title: Shocking! Voltura Fiat 500 Quietly Redefines the Restomod

body_markdown:
In a world where the price of a premium restomod can run into seven figures, and might be accompanied by a four-figure horsepower rating, Voltura is a breath of fresh air. Quite literally, in fact, as its cars have no exhaust.


Based in Wiltshire, England,[Voltura](https://www.voltura-cars.com/) takes the classic[Fiat Cinquecento](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-buyers-guide-1957-75-fiat-500-buyers-guide/) , built from 1957 to 1975, and gives it a fully electric powertrain, modern lighting, brakes, instrumentation, and infotainment system. The company was created in 2024, “founded by a team of restoration specialists, EV engineers and product designers who believed the Fiat 500 deserved more than a museum shelf — it deserved another life.”


It represents the next stage in central founder Jack Kerridge’s plan to create “the best Fiat 500 in the world.” Having previously founded[Silent Classics](https://www.silentclassics.co.uk/) , which provides EV conversion kits, Kerridge now wants to build complete cars. Initially these will be restored and updated originals, but soon he believes Voltura will be able to supply completely new vehicles.


“All the parts are still available, and reasonably priced,” he explains. “The only thing you can’t get new is the roof. I really want to offer something which is more affordable and the only way to do that is to make it ourselves; otherwise, you just can’t get around the potential thousands of hours of restoration.”


For now, though, the workshop in Warminster, England—about a hundred miles west of London, and not far from the prehistoric monoliths of Stonehenge—is full of original 500s in various stages of recovery and reimagination.


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


“I think it’s an underrated, beautiful shape, and if it’s presented well, I think it’s a piece of art,” says Kerridge. “But I don’t think that what makes this a beautiful car has anything to do with the engine. In my opinion, it sounds like a lawnmower. I think it actually lets the car down, so it’s a perfect candidate \[for electrification\].”


Voltura’s first U.S. customers, who are due to take delivery of their car in San Francisco in November, would appear to agree. “They went out to Tuscany and they took a Fiat 500 tour, and they just fell in love with the car. Then they found us and were amazed, saying, ‘Oh my god, you literally just get in there, turn it on, and drive it.’”


Voltura


Dyed-in-the-wool British Cinquecento fans have also been converted, says Kerridge. “We had a couple come along in their car, saying that they were curious but really didn’t think it would be a 500 without the engine. Then they went for a drive. When they came back, they put down a deposit immediately.”


[I drove a Silent Classics–converted car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/driving/ev-swapped-fiat-500-drives-home-the-virtues-of-silence-and-smiles/) in 2023 and liked it. However, I felt the initial pickup could be improved, the regenerative braking would have benefited from a bit more oomph, and that it wasn’t quite as silent as the name implied, with the retained gearbox and differential whining away.


Now there’s a completely new conversion kit based around a 35 kW (47 hp) AC induction motor, with an integrated 6:1 reduction gearbox. Two battery options are available: a 13.7-kWh City version with a range of 80 miles, and a Rural pack with 21.5 kWh capacity that can do 140 miles.


It’s early in the Voltura business, so the car that showcases all the exterior and interior updates doesn’t have the new powertrain. Instead, it’ll be an unrestored development hack that I’m taking out for a spin.


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


[Nik Berg](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/nberg/)


The development car is a big step up from the first Silent Classics conversion, with instant, eager acceleration up to 30 mph, which then trails off a tad as the torque is reduced. Nonetheless, it will get to 60 mph in under ten seconds (some 20 seconds quicker than a twin-cylinder car), and I come close to its top speed of 65 mph on a straight stretch of road.


Now there really is almost no noise from the powertrain after the initial takeoff, and it zips through country lanes with only the sound of the wind rushing through the open canvas top. The brakes are punchier, thanks to a disc upgrade and some pedal adjustment, and the regeneration is more effective. Kerridge is also experimenting with rack and pinion steering, and it’s certainly less woolly than standard.

It’s a shame that I can’t quite get the full Voltura experience, with all the cosmetic and comfort upgrades fitted to a mint green model in the workshop. Kerridge has created new door cards, a whole new center console with integrated armrest, a turnwheel gear selector, and cupholders. The single circular driver’s display is digital, and there’s even a CarPlay-compatible audio system. Brown leather and aluminum are the materials of choice, with Kerridge himself sculpting the metal indicator stalks. It’s all rather lovely.


For the outside, Kerridge de-seamed the body for a smoother finish and better rust resistance, installed closer-fitting bumpers front and rear, and updated the lights to LEDs. Unless you saw it plugged in, you wouldn’t guess it’s electric.


Voltura


Voltura


Voltura


On that subject, Volturas are not DC fast-charge ready, but the battery packs are small enough that four hours on U.K. standard AC electricity will deliver a full charge. That would make extended road trips a challenge, but Kerridge foresees most customers using their cars in cities and for short weekend jaunts.


In fact, it’s the smaller battery option that Voltura’s first American drivers have opted for, so don’t expect to see it straying too far from San Francisco when it hits the road later this year.


For legal reasons, the car will be shipped with the powertrain removed and supplied separately, and then Voltura’s U.S. installation partner, California’s[Z Electric Motors](https://www.zelectricmotors.com/) , will re-fit it. It’s a process that takes just a day or so and is also reversible.


Given the specification of this first car, the price is on the high side, but still under $100,000. Conversion kits begin at under $22,000, and if all goes according to plan, Voltura’s “new” 500s will be much more affordable.
